questions.questionText: What does full fine-tuning require that makes it expensive for large models?
options: Nothing extra, it's the cheapest fine-tuning approach
GPU memory to store gradients and optimizer state for every single weight in the model, plus a full model copy per fine-tuned variant
It only works on CPUs, never GPUs
It requires no training data at all
questions.correctAnswer: GPU memory to store gradients and optimizer state for every single weight in the model, plus a full model copy per fine-tuned variant
questions.explanation: Updating every weight means storing gradient and optimizer state proportional to the entire model's parameter count, which scales expensively for billion-parameter models.

questions.questionText: What does LoRA actually train, while the original model's weights stay frozen?
options: It retrains every weight, just more slowly
Small, low-rank additional matrices added on top of specific weight matrices, dramatically smaller than the original weights
A completely separate model from scratch
questions.correctAnswer: Small, low-rank additional matrices added on top of specific weight matrices, dramatically smaller than the original weights
questions.explanation: LoRA freezes the pretrained weights entirely and trains small add-on matrices (A and B) whose product approximates the needed adaptation, at a small fraction of the original parameter count.

questions.questionText: What key insight does LoRA rely on to work well despite training so few parameters?
options: That most tasks require completely reshaping the model's behavior
That the change needed to adapt a model to a new task typically has much lower intrinsic complexity than the model's full weight matrix
That gradients don't matter for fine-tuning
That frozen weights automatically adapt themselves
questions.correctAnswer: That the change needed to adapt a model to a new task typically has much lower intrinsic complexity than the model's full weight matrix
questions.explanation: This low intrinsic-rank assumption is what lets small A/B matrices capture most of the useful adaptation, without needing to update the full, much larger weight matrix.
